title: Interest on client money
subtitle: The duty to account for a fair sum, without a prescribed rate or a fixed formula
objectives: State the duty under r 7 to account to a client for a fair sum of interest on client money held, and explain that the SRA does not prescribe a rate
Explain why firms are expected to hold a written interest policy, and what makes a policy term fair rather than merely convenient for the firm
Apply a firm's de minimis threshold to a set of facts to determine whether interest must be calculated and paid over on a given holding

leadingAuthorities.role: Imposes the duty to account for a fair sum of interest on client money held, on whatever basis a written policy sets out

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Most students assume there must be a fixed statutory interest rate somewhere, the way there is for judgment debts. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this note appears: 'You know there's no fixed rate — this lesson is about what firms actually have to do instead.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on the underlying principle here before. The test pool below leans on applying a firm's own policy and threshold to specific holdings — expect figures and time periods, not just the headline rule.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and Part 2 and make sure you can say clearly what r 7 does and does not require before moving on — the rest of the lesson builds on that gap between duty and discretion.

overview.hook: A firm holds £400,000 of a client's money for four months while a property chain completes. The client later asks: how much interest did you earn for me on that? The honest answer is not a number pulled from a statute — it is 'whatever our written policy says a fair sum is', and that answer is deliberately not the same at every firm.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 24 September 2026. The SRA's approach — a duty to pay a fair sum with no prescribed rate or method — has been stable since the 2019 Accounts Rules came into force and is not currently under review. What does vary, lawfully, from firm to firm is the rate a policy sets and the threshold below which interest need not be calculated at all; this lesson treats that variation as the deliberate design of the rule, not an unresolved question.

parts.heading: A duty with no number attached
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the puzzle before resolving it
body: Ask a new trainee what interest rate a firm must pay a client on money held in the client account, and the honest first guess is usually a number — base rate, a percentage, something fixed. There isn't one. SRA Accounts Rules 2019, r 7 requires a firm to account to the client for a fair sum of interest on client money it holds, but the rules deliberately say nothing about what rate, formula, or calculation method makes a sum 'fair'.

That silence is not a gap in the rules — it is the rule. The SRA regulates outcomes (clients must not be left out of pocket by a firm banking their money and keeping any benefit) without prescribing the mechanics, because firms hold enormously different types and volumes of client money, at different banks, on different account structures, and a single fixed formula would either overpay some clients at the firm's expense or underpay others.

What fills the gap instead is each firm's own written interest policy: a document setting the rate (or a defensible method of calculating one, often tracking a nominated bank's rate), the de minimis threshold below which interest is not calculated, and how and when interest is paid over. Every firm must have one; no two firms' policies need to be identical.

components.definition: The r 7 standard for interest on client money: not a fixed statutory rate, but whatever amount a firm's own reasonable, transparent, written interest policy produces when applied honestly to the money actually held.

interaction.prompt: Name the SRA Accounts Rules 2019 provision that requires a firm to account to a client for interest on client money it holds.
interaction.modelAnswer: SRA Accounts Rules 2019, r 7 — the duty to account to the client for a fair sum of interest on client money held, with no prescribed rate.

parts.heading: Why the SRA doesn't set a rate
parts.voice: argumentative — states the strongest case for the flexible standard, then tests it
body: It's worth taking seriously why a fixed rate would actually be worse for clients, not just administratively inconvenient for firms. Client money sits in different places: a general client account pooling many clients' money together, or occasionally a designated deposit account for one client's larger sum. It earns different rates depending on the bank, the account type, and prevailing market conditions, which shift over the life of a long-running matter.

A single SRA-mandated rate, fixed by regulation, would quickly become either too generous (forcing firms to pay out more than the money actually earned, effectively subsidising clients from the firm's own funds) or too stingy (letting firms retain a real benefit that was earned by holding the client's money). Tying the duty instead to a fair sum, assessed against what the firm's own banking arrangements actually produced, keeps the obligation honest to the real economics of each holding.

The trade-off is that 'fair' has to be policed by transparency rather than by a bright line: a firm's policy has to be written down, available to clients, and applied consistently — not adjusted case by case to suit the firm. A policy that quietly pays less to clients whose money is held longest, with no honest banking justification, would fail the fair sum standard even though no rate in the rules was technically breached.

components.label: What a compliant interest policy typically covers
points: The rate or method used to calculate interest (often tracking a nominated clearing bank's published rate)
The de minimis threshold below which the firm will not calculate or pay interest
How interest is calculated across a general client account holding several clients' money at once
When and how interest is paid over to the client — typically on completion of the matter or at agreed intervals
That the policy is available to clients on request, and applied consistently rather than case by case

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that the SRA prescribes a fixed interest rate that all firms must apply to client money?
sliderLabels: Definitely does not prescribe a rate
interaction.explanation: No fixed rate exists. R 7 sets the standard — a fair sum — and leaves the rate and method to each firm's own written, transparent policy, assessed against the real banking arrangements behind the money actually held.

parts.heading: The de minimis threshold: when interest need not be calculated at all
parts.voice: direct — works through the mechanics with figures
body: A firm need not calculate or pay interest at all where the amount involved is small enough, or the period short enough, that doing so would cost more in administrative effort than the sum is worth — this is the de minimis threshold, and it is itself a term the firm's own policy sets, not a figure fixed by the SRA.

A realistic example: a firm's policy sets a de minimis threshold of interest amounts under £50. It holds £2,000 for a client for three weeks while a straightforward matter concludes. At a plausible policy rate, that produces perhaps £2–03 of interest — comfortably under the threshold, so the firm is not obliged to calculate or pay it. Change the facts to £350,000 held for four months, and even a modest rate produces a sum firmly above any sensible threshold — the duty to calculate and account for it bites in full.

The threshold has to be set at a genuinely de minimis level to be defensible — a policy setting the threshold at, say, £1,000 to sweep most ordinary client holdings out of scope would struggle to be called fair, because it would be designed to avoid the duty rather than to avoid disproportionate administration on genuinely trivial sums.

components.text: A firm must account to the client, or third party, for a fair sum of interest on any client money held on their behalf. A firm may, by way of a written policy available to the client, set a threshold below which interest need not be calculated, provided the threshold and the underlying rate or method are genuinely designed to reflect what is fair, rather than to minimise what the firm pays out.
elements: Duty to account for a fair sum of interest
Applies to client money held on the client's or a third party's behalf
A written, available policy may set a genuine de minimis threshold
The threshold and method must be fair, not designed to defeat the duty

interaction.prompt: Put these steps in the order a firm should actually follow when deciding whether interest is payable on a holding.
items: Identify how much client money is held and for how long
Apply the firm's written policy rate or method to calculate the interest that sum would produce
Compare the calculated interest against the policy's de minimis threshold
If above the threshold, account to the client for the fair sum; if below, no payment is required
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the sequence: you calculate first, then test against the threshold — the threshold is a filter on the result, not a shortcut that skips the calculation.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order — the firm has to work out what interest the holding would actually produce before it can compare that figure against its de minimis threshold.

parts.heading: What a fair policy is not
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells a short scenario before naming the doctrine it breaches
body: A firm's finance director notices that client account interest income, if simply retained by the firm rather than paid out below a generous threshold, would meaningfully boost the firm's annual profit. The director proposes raising the de minimis threshold from £50 to £500, reasoning that 'most client holdings fall under £500 anyway, so this simplifies our bookkeeping considerably.'

This is the point where a plausible-sounding administrative justification masks a breach of the fair sum standard. The test is not whether a threshold change reduces the firm's workload — it is whether the threshold reflects a genuine judgement about what is disproportionate to calculate, applied consistently and transparently. A threshold set specifically because it sweeps most client holdings out of scope, motivated by the resulting benefit to the firm, fails that test even if it is written down and even if clients are nominally told about it.

Contrast a firm that reviews its threshold periodically against actual banking costs and concludes £50 remains proportionate — or one that lowers it as its systems become more automated and cheaper to run. Both of those are defensible exercises of the same discretion the rule grants; the finance director's proposal is not, because its purpose is to benefit the firm at clients' expense rather than to avoid disproportionate administration.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often assume that because the SRA does not fix a threshold figure, any threshold a firm chooses and writes down is automatically compliant.
components.whyItsWrong: Discretion under r 7 is bounded by the fair sum standard itself. A written policy is necessary but not sufficient — the rate and threshold it sets still have to be genuinely justifiable as fair, not merely documented. A threshold chosen to minimise payouts to clients, rather than to avoid disproportionate administration, breaches the duty even though it is in writing.

interaction.prompt: In the passage below, highlight the sentence that states why the finance director's proposal is not compliant.
interaction.passage: The firm's proposal raises the de minimis threshold to £500. Writing a threshold down and telling clients about it satisfies the transparency element of r 7, but transparency alone is not enough. A threshold set specifically because it sweeps most client holdings out of scope, motivated by the resulting benefit to the firm, fails the fair sum standard even though it is written down and disclosed.
interaction.ratioSentence: A threshold set specifically because it sweeps most client holdings out of scope, motivated by the resulting benefit to the firm, fails the fair sum standard even though it is written down and disclosed.

parts.heading: Applying the duty to a running matter
parts.voice: worked example — walks the reasoning through a realistic timeline
body: Put the pieces together on a single matter. A firm receives £180,000 into its client account from a client selling a property, pending completion of the client's onward purchase six weeks later. The firm's written policy sets a de minimis threshold of £25 and a rate tracking its nominated bank's published rate for balances of that size.

At the policy rate, £180,000 held for six weeks produces a calculated interest figure comfortably above the £25 threshold — so the duty to account for it is live from the moment the calculation is done, not merely from the moment the client asks. The firm does not need the client to request interest, and it does not need a court order or a complaint to trigger the obligation: r 7 imposes it as a standing duty on money the firm holds.

When completion happens six weeks later and the balance is paid out to the client (or applied to the purchase), the calculated interest is paid over alongside it, without the client needing to ask, negotiate, or even know in advance that the firm had been tracking the figure throughout.

components.label: What triggers the duty to pay
points: The duty is standing, not request-based — it does not depend on the client asking for interest
It applies once the calculated sum, against the firm's own policy, exceeds the de minimis threshold
Payment is typically made when the money is paid out or the matter concludes, not only on request
The firm cannot avoid the duty simply by not mentioning interest is being tracked

interaction.prompt: A firm holds £90,000 for a client for five weeks pending a property completion, then pays the balance out without mentioning interest. The client never asked about it. The firm's policy sets a £30 de minimis threshold, and the calculated interest on this holding is £47. Analyse whether the firm has complied with r 7.
factsToOrder: The firm holds £90,000 for five weeks
The calculated interest is £47, above the threshold
The firm paid out the balance without mentioning or paying the interest
The client never asked about interest

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the firm has complied with its r 7 duty to account for a fair sum of interest on the £90,000 held.
modelAnswer.rule: R 7 imposes a standing duty to account for a fair sum of interest on client money held, assessed against the firm's own written policy; the duty does not depend on the client requesting it, and only falls away where the calculated sum is below the firm's genuine de minimis threshold.
modelAnswer.application: The calculated interest of £47 exceeds the firm's own £30 threshold, so the duty to account for it is live on the firm's own policy terms. That the client never asked is irrelevant — the duty is standing, not request-based. Paying out the balance without paying or even mentioning the interest leaves the client out of pocket by the amount the firm's own policy says is due.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The firm has not complied with r 7: it should have calculated and paid over the £47 interest alongside the balance, regardless of whether the client asked.

testPool.prompt: Does SRA Accounts Rules 2019, r 7 fix a specific interest rate that all firms must apply to client money held?
options: No — it requires a fair sum, with the rate and method left to each firm's own written policy
Yes — it sets a rate tied to the Bank of England base rate
Yes — it fixes a flat 2% rate for all client money
No — because r 7 does not apply to interest at all
testPool.explanation: R 7 sets a standard (a fair sum) rather than a fixed rate. Each firm's own written policy sets the rate or method, which can lawfully differ between firms.

testPool.prompt: A client asks a trainee why their firm's interest policy pays a different rate from a rival firm down the road. Which is the correct explanation?
options: One of the two firms must be breaching r 7, since the rate should be identical everywhere
Both can be lawful — r 7 requires a fair sum assessed against each firm's own banking arrangements, not an identical rate across the profession
Only firms holding money in a designated deposit account are entitled to set their own rate
The rate is set by the SRA annually and republished; any difference must be an administrative error
testPool.explanation: Because r 7 does not prescribe a single rate, lawful variation between firms is expected — it reflects genuine differences in banking arrangements, not a breach by either firm.

testPool.prompt: A firm's written interest policy sets a de minimis threshold of £600, on the stated basis that this sweeps almost all its client holdings out of scope and meaningfully reduces its finance team's workload. Is this threshold likely to satisfy the fair sum standard?
options: Yes — any threshold is compliant provided it is written down and disclosed to clients
No — a threshold chosen because it sweeps most holdings out of scope, rather than because it reflects genuinely disproportionate administration on trivial sums, is unlikely to be fair
Yes — workload reduction is always a legitimate basis for setting a threshold at any level
No — de minimis thresholds are not permitted under r 7 at all
testPool.trapExplanation: Writing the threshold down and telling clients satisfies transparency, but transparency is not the whole test. A threshold set to minimise what the firm pays out, rather than to avoid genuinely disproportionate administration, fails the fair sum standard regardless of disclosure.
testPool.explanation: The stated rationale — reducing payouts by sweeping most holdings out of scope — is exactly the kind of purpose the fair sum standard is designed to catch, even though a de minimis threshold is in principle permitted.

testPool.prompt: A firm calculates that a client holding would earn £18 in interest, which falls below its £25 de minimis threshold. The firm therefore pays nothing and does not tell the client any calculation was done. Has the firm breached r 7?
options: Yes — the firm must always disclose that a calculation was performed, even below the threshold
No — provided the threshold is a genuine, fair one, the firm is not obliged to calculate, pay, or specifically flag amounts that fall below it
Yes — any de minimis threshold below £50 is automatically unfair
No, but only because the client never asked about interest
testPool.trapExplanation: It's tempting to think transparency requires disclosing every calculation, however small. It doesn't — a genuine de minimis threshold exists precisely so the firm need not calculate, pay, or flag amounts below it; the policy itself (not each individual sub-threshold figure) is what must be available to clients.
testPool.explanation: Provided £25 is a genuinely defensible threshold on this firm's facts, no breach arises from not paying or flagging an £18 figure that falls below it.

testPool.prompt: A firm holds £220,000 for a client for eight weeks pending a corporate completion. Its policy threshold is £40, and the calculated interest on this holding is £310. The matter concludes and the balance is paid out; the client had not mentioned interest at any point. What should the firm do?
options: Pay out the balance only — no obligation arises until the client specifically requests interest
Calculate and pay over the £310 interest alongside the balance, without waiting for a request
Retain the £310 as it falls within the firm's discretion to keep amounts under £500
Pay only half the calculated interest, since the client never chased the matter
testPool.explanation: £310 is well above the £40 threshold, so the standing duty under r 7 is live. It does not depend on the client asking — the firm must calculate and account for the fair sum as a matter of course.

testPool.prompt: A firm holds £4,500 for a client for nine days while a straightforward matter concludes. Its policy threshold is £50, and the calculated interest at the policy rate is £1.40. Has the firm complied with r 7 if it pays out the balance without calculating or paying any interest?
options: No — any positive interest figure, however small, must be paid
Yes — £1.40 falls below the firm's genuine £50 threshold, so no payment is required
No — the firm should have raised its threshold before relying on it
Yes, but only because the holding period was under ten days
testPool.explanation: £1.40 is comfortably below the £50 threshold, so provided that threshold is genuine and fair, the firm is not obliged to calculate or pay it — this is exactly the scenario the de minimis threshold exists to cover.

testPool.prompt: A firm's policy sets a de minimis threshold of £30. It holds £55,000 for a client for three weeks; the calculated interest is £29.60. Payment is due to the client tomorrow. What is the firm's obligation regarding the £29.60?
options: It must be paid, since it is close to the threshold and the firm should round in the client's favour as a matter of good practice
It falls below the £30 threshold, so no payment is strictly required, though many firms would pay it anyway as a matter of client care
It must be doubled and paid, as a penalty for the firm holding money so close to the threshold
The firm must ask the client whether they want it paid or not
testPool.explanation: £29.60 falls just under the £30 threshold, so strictly no payment is required under r 7. Many firms choose to pay marginal amounts anyway for goodwill, but that is a business choice, not a rule requirement.

testPool.prompt: Under SRA Accounts Rules 2019, r 7, which of the following must a firm's written interest policy address for the firm to comply?
options: The specific individual client's investment risk appetite
The rate or method used to calculate interest, and a genuine de minimis threshold if one is applied
The firm's total annual profit from banking arrangements
A guarantee that interest will always exceed the Bank of England base rate
testPool.explanation: A compliant policy addresses the rate or calculation method and, if used, a genuine threshold — not the client's personal risk appetite, the firm's overall profit, or any guaranteed minimum tied to base rate.

testPool.prompt: A firm never writes an interest policy down, but says it has always paid interest 'fairly, on a case-by-case basis, using its best judgement.' Does this comply with r 7?
options: Yes — r 7 only requires a fair outcome, and the method used to reach it is irrelevant
No — a case-by-case, undocumented approach fails the transparency and consistency expected of a fair sum policy, even if individual outcomes happen to be generous
Yes, provided the firm can show at least one client was paid more than the calculated market rate
No, but only because case-by-case decisions are always numerically less generous than a written policy
testPool.explanation: The fair sum standard is policed through a written, consistently applied policy precisely because case-by-case discretion, however well-intentioned, cannot be checked or relied on by clients in the same way — an undocumented approach falls short even if individual results happen to be fair.

testPool.prompt: A firm's policy correctly calculates interest on client money held in its general client account, which pools several clients' money together. Which statement best describes how this pooling affects the r 7 duty?
options: Pooling removes the duty entirely, since no individual client's money can be separately identified
The duty still applies to each client's share of the pooled money, calculated on a fair and consistent basis even though the underlying bank account is not client-specific
Only the client with the largest balance in the pooled account is owed interest
Interest is only payable on money held in a separate designated deposit account, never in a general client account
testPool.explanation: Pooling money for banking convenience does not remove the underlying duty to each client — a compliant policy allocates a fair, consistently calculated share to each client whose money contributed to the pooled balance.

testPool.prompt: A client complains that no interest was paid on £12,000 held for six weeks. The firm's policy threshold is £20, and the calculated interest is £18.90. The client argues the firm must pay because £18.90 is 'obviously a real amount of money, not nothing.' Is the client's argument correct?
options: Yes — any calculable positive figure must be paid regardless of the policy threshold
No — provided the £20 threshold is a genuine, fair one, an amount below it need not be paid, whatever the client's subjective view of its significance
Yes, because £18.90 exceeds £10 and any threshold below £10 is automatically unlawful
No, but only because the client did not raise the point before the matter concluded
testPool.trapExplanation: It's tempting to sympathise with the client's plain-English objection that £18.90 clearly isn't nothing. But the fair sum standard is tested against the genuineness of the threshold itself, not against a client's individual view of what counts as a meaningful sum.
testPool.explanation: Provided the £20 threshold reflects genuine, fair reasoning about disproportionate administration, an amount below it need not be paid — the client's characterisation of the sum as 'real money' does not itself change the analysis.

testPool.prompt: A firm pays interest to clients only when the client specifically asks for it in writing, reasoning that this saves unnecessary administration on matters where no one raises the point. Is this practice compliant with r 7?
options: Yes — the duty is only triggered once a client makes a request
No — the r 7 duty is standing and does not depend on a client request; the firm must calculate and pay where the fair sum exceeds its own threshold, request or not
Yes, provided the firm's terms of business mention that interest is 'available on request'
No, but only for corporate clients — individual clients must always ask first
testPool.trapExplanation: Making interest conditional on a request sounds like reasonable administrative practice, but it inverts the duty: r 7 places the burden on the firm to calculate and pay proactively, not on the client to know to ask.
testPool.explanation: A request-only practice breaches r 7 wherever it results in a fair sum going uncalculated or unpaid on holdings that exceed the firm's own threshold — the duty does not wait for the client to raise it.

testPool.prompt: Must a firm's interest policy be the same for every type of client money it holds (for example, conveyancing completion funds versus probate estate funds)?
options: No — a policy can reasonably differ by account type or holding pattern, provided each element remains genuinely fair and is applied consistently within its own terms
Yes — r 7 requires one uniform rate and threshold across all client money a firm holds, regardless of type
Yes, but only because the SRA publishes a single approved rate table
No, but only for firms with more than one office
testPool.explanation: R 7 does not require uniformity across every category of holding — what matters is that whatever terms apply are genuinely fair and consistently applied, not that a single figure covers every kind of client money.

testPool.prompt: A firm's policy states a de minimis threshold of £50 'reviewed annually against actual banking costs', and the firm can show the figure has moved down twice in the past five years as its systems became cheaper to run. A client's holding produces £42 in calculated interest, below the threshold, and no payment is made. Applying r 7, is this most likely compliant?
options: No — any threshold above £25 is automatically unfair regardless of how it was set

Yes — a threshold genuinely reviewed against real administrative cost, and moving in the client's favour over time, is consistent with the fair sum standard even though this particular £42 goes unpaid
No — the threshold must be reduced to zero once a firm's systems are automated
Yes, but only if the client is told about the review policy before the matter starts
testPool.explanation: A threshold with a documented, cost-based justification that moves in the client's favour over time is exactly the kind of genuine, defensible policy r 7 contemplates — the fact that one client's £42 falls just under it does not, by itself, indicate unfairness.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The single most common mistake in this lesson's test items is assuming that because there is no fixed rate, a firm has free rein — or, in the opposite direction, that any positive interest figure must always be paid. Neither is right: the fair sum standard bites on the genuineness of the firm's own policy and threshold, applied consistently, whether or not the client ever asks.
